title: LLM Alignment Series: Proximal Policy Optimization
text:
2026-03-08
When Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) was introduced in 2017, much of deep reinforcement learning was focused on high-dimensional control problems. The original PPO paper (Schulman, Wolski, et al. 2017) evaluated the method on benchmark tasks that included continuous control in MuJoCo and discrete environments such as Atari. At the time, reinforcement learning was shaped mainly by deep Q-learning, vanilla policy gradient methods, and trust region policy optimization (TRPO) (Schulman, Levine, et al. 2017). These methods had already shown strong results, but they also revealed a practical gap: the field still lacked a policy optimization method that was stable, sample-efficient, and easy to train with standard neural network pipelines.
PPO was introduced as a practical answer to that problem. It kept the central motivation behind TRPO (see my previous post LLM Alignment Series: Trust Region Policy Optimization), namely controlling the size of policy updates, but replaced TRPO’s more complicated constrained optimization procedure with a simpler objective that could be optimized using ordinary first-order methods. In the original experiments, PPO performed well on robotic locomotion tasks, where simulated humanoids learned to run, steer, and recover from perturbations. These results showed that the method could handle continuous action spaces and fairly complex dynamics without sacrificing training stability.
The same design choices that made PPO effective in robotic control later made it useful for large-scale language model alignment. TRPO offered stronger theoretical machinery, but in practice it depended on second-order approximations and conjugate gradient steps that were awkward to incorporate into standard deep learning workflows. PPO simplified this setup by introducing a clipped surrogate objective that serves as a practical approximation to trust-region-style updates while remaining fully compatible with first-order optimization. In PPO, training alternates between collecting data and performing several epochs of stochastic gradient updates on that same batch.
When large transformer language models became the focus of alignment work, these properties made PPO a natural choice for reinforcement learning from human feedback. With models containing billions of parameters, second-order optimization is generally too expensive to be practical. At the same time, fine-tuning must remain stable enough to improve behavior without damaging the linguistic structure learned during pretraining. PPO offered a workable tradeoff: it constrained policy updates through clipping, allowed multiple updates on the same batch, and fit naturally into existing deep learning training systems. What began as a method for stabilizing reinforcement learning in simulated control environments later became one of the central optimization methods used in RLHF.

title: LLM Alignment Series: Proximal Policy Optimization
text:
1 Clipped Surrogate Objective
To understand how PPO extracts multiple optimization steps from a single batch of experience, we need to examine the mathematical mechanism that governs its updates: the probability ratio and the clipped surrogate objective.

1.1 The Probability Ratio
The construction begins with the probability ratio:
r_t(\theta) = \frac{\pi_\theta(a_t \mid s_t)}{\pi_{\theta_{\text{old}}}(a_t \mid s_t)}
This quantity compares how likely the current policy \pi_\theta is to select action a_t in state s_t relative to the policy \pi_{\theta_{\text{old}}} that originally generated the data. In effect, the ratio serves as an importance sampling correction. Since the trajectories were collected under an older policy, the ratio adjusts the learning signal so that updates remain valid for the current policy parameters.
If we multiply this ratio by an advantage estimate \hat{A}_t, we recover the conservative policy iteration objective:
L^{CPI}(\theta) = \hat{\mathbb{E}}_t \left[ r_t(\theta) \hat{A}_t \right]
This formulation appears in earlier policy gradient methods and can be interpreted as an off-policy correction for policy updates. However, maximizing this objective without additional constraints can lead to unstable learning. When an action receives a large positive advantage estimate, gradient ascent will aggressively increase its probability, potentially causing the policy to change too drastically in a single update.


1.2 The Clipped Surrogate Objective
Earlier work addressed this instability using trust-region constraints, most notably in Trust Region Policy Optimization (TRPO). PPO takes a different approach. Instead of explicitly enforcing a KL-divergence constraint, it introduces a clipped surrogate objective that restricts how far the probability ratio can deviate from 1.
A small hyperparameter \epsilon, typically set to 0.2, defines the allowable update region. The ratio is effectively constrained by the interval [1-\epsilon, 1+\epsilon].
This leads to the PPO surrogate objective:
L^{CLIP}(\theta) = \hat{\mathbb{E}}_t \left[ \min \left( r_t(\theta) \hat{A}_t, \text{clip}(r_t(\theta), 1-\epsilon, 1+\epsilon) \hat{A}_t \right) \right]
The key design choice is the minimum operator between the unclipped objective and the clipped version. This creates a pessimistic bound: the algorithm always chooses the smaller of the two values. As a result, the optimization process avoids updates that would excessively increase the policy ratio beyond the safe region.


1.3 Asymmetric Stabilization
The effect becomes clearer when considering the behavior based on the advantage sign.
If the advantage is positive, the update encourages the policy to increase the probability of the chosen action. As the probability ratio approaches 1+\epsilon, the clipped objective stops increasing. Beyond this point, further increases in probability no longer improve the objective, effectively preventing overly large updates.
If the advantage is negative, the policy should reduce the probability of the action. When the ratio drops below 1-\epsilon, the clipped objective again flattens, limiting further decreases.
An important property of this construction is its asymmetry. The clipping mechanism suppresses updates that would make the objective appear artificially better, while still allowing updates that reduce the objective when the policy change would be harmful. In practice, this acts as a stabilizing mechanism that discourages overly optimistic policy updates while still permitting corrective adjustments. Through this modification, PPO approximates the stabilizing behavior of trust-region methods without requiring second-order optimization or explicit KL constraints.

title: LLM Alignment Series: Proximal Policy Optimization
text:
2 Generalized Advantage Estimation
The core quantity driving the policy update in Proximal Policy Optimization is the advantage estimate, denoted by \hat{A}_t. This quantity serves as the signal that evaluates whether a chosen action performed better or worse than expected. In theory, the advantage function is defined as the difference between the action-value function and the state-value function,
A^\pi(s_t, a_t) = Q^\pi(s_t, a_t) - V^\pi(s_t)
It measures how much better or worse action a_t is, relative to the baseline value of state s_t. Within PPO’s surrogate objective, this advantage estimate directly scales the probability ratio. If \hat{A}_t is positive, the optimization process is encouraged to increase the probability of that action. If \hat{A}_t is negative, the algorithm instead reduces its probability.
In practice, PPO does not compute the exact theoretical advantage. Instead, it relies on Generalized Advantage Estimation (GAE), which provides a practical compromise between high-variance Monte Carlo returns and high-bias temporal-difference learning. The starting point of GAE is the one-step temporal-difference residual,
\delta_t = r_t + \gamma V(s_{t+1}) - V(s_t)
This term can be interpreted as the one-step Bellman error under the current value estimate. Rather than using only this single-step quantity, GAE constructs the advantage estimate as an exponentially weighted sum of future temporal-difference residuals. For a trajectory segment, this gives
\hat{A}_t = \delta_t + (\gamma \lambda)\delta_{t+1} + (\gamma \lambda)^2 \delta_{t+2} + \cdots
Equivalently,
\hat{A}_t = \sum_{l=0}^{T-t-1} (\gamma \lambda)^l \delta_{t+l}
The parameter \lambda \in [0,1] controls the bias-variance tradeoff. When \lambda is close to 1, the estimator behaves more like a Monte Carlo return: it has lower bias but higher variance. When \lambda is smaller, the estimate relies more heavily on the learned value function, which reduces variance at the cost of introducing additional bias. In this way, GAE provides a flexible mechanism for stabilizing policy gradient training.
The quality of these advantage estimates depends critically on the accuracy of the value function. For this reason, PPO trains a value network, or critic, alongside the policy. The critic is optimized through a squared-error objective of the form
L_t^{VF}(\theta) = \left( V_\theta(s_t) - V_t^{\mathrm{targ}} \right)^2
Here, V_t^{\mathrm{targ}} denotes a target return constructed from observed rewards, typically using discounted returns or a bootstrapped target. Minimizing this loss improves the critic’s estimate of expected future return from each state.
This value learning component is not merely auxiliary. As the critic becomes more accurate, the baseline V(s_t) becomes more reliable, which in turn produces cleaner temporal-difference residuals \delta_t. Those improved residuals yield more accurate advantage estimates \hat{A}_t, and those more accurate advantages provide a better learning signal for the actor. PPO therefore operates through a tightly coupled interaction between policy improvement and value estimation: the critic stabilizes the gradient signal, and the actor uses that signal to improve the policy. The result is a learning process in which value estimation and policy optimization reinforce one another throughout training.

2.1 From TD Residuals to the GAE Estimator
The clipped surrogate objective in PPO determines how aggressively the policy is allowed to change, but that objective is only as reliable as the advantage estimates that feed into it. To understand why PPO remains stable in practice, we therefore need to examine how those advantages are constructed.
We begin with the theoretical definition of the advantage function. Under a policy \pi, the advantage of taking action a_t in state s_t is

A^\pi(s_t, a_t) = Q^\pi(s_t, a_t) - V^\pi(s_t).

This quantity measures how much better or worse an action is relative to the baseline value of the current state. In practice, however, the action-value function Q^\pi(s_t, a_t) is not directly available and must be estimated from sampled trajectories.
A natural way to approximate it is through a family of k-step empirical returns. The one-step return is

R_t^{(1)} = r_t + \gamma V(s_{t+1}),

the two-step return is

R_t^{(2)} = r_t + \gamma r_{t+1} + \gamma^2 V(s_{t+2}),

and the general k-step return is

R_t^{(k)} = \sum_{l=0}^{k-1} \gamma^l r_{t+l} + \gamma^k V(s_{t+k}).

Subtracting the baseline V(s_t) from each return gives a corresponding sequence of k-step advantage estimators.
For the one-step case, we obtain

\hat{A}_t^{(1)} = R_t^{(1)} - V(s_t)
= r_t + \gamma V(s_{t+1}) - V(s_t).

This is exactly the one-step temporal-difference residual,

\delta_t = r_t + \gamma V(s_{t+1}) - V(s_t).

Thus,

\hat{A}_t^{(1)} = \delta_t.

For the two-step case, the estimator becomes

\hat{A}_t^{(2)} = R_t^{(2)} - V(s_t)
= r_t + \gamma r_{t+1} + \gamma^2 V(s_{t+2}) - V(s_t).

By adding and subtracting the intermediate term \gamma V(s_{t+1}), this can be rearranged as

\hat{A}_t^{(2)}
= \bigl(r_t + \gamma V(s_{t+1}) - V(s_t)\bigr)
+ \gamma \bigl(r_{t+1} + \gamma V(s_{t+2}) - V(s_{t+1})\bigr),

which simplifies to

\hat{A}_t^{(2)} = \delta_t + \gamma \delta_{t+1}.

The same pattern extends to longer horizons. In general, the k-step estimator can be written as

\hat{A}_t^{(k)} = \sum_{l=0}^{k-1} \gamma^l \delta_{t+l}.

This expression reveals an important structural fact: multi-step advantage estimation is built entirely from discounted sums of TD residuals. As the horizon k increases, the estimator depends on more realized rewards and less on immediate bootstrapping. This tends to reduce bias, but it also increases variance because more stochasticity from the trajectory is accumulated.
Generalized Advantage Estimation addresses this tradeoff by taking an exponentially weighted average over all k-step estimators. With a decay parameter \lambda \in [0,1], GAE is defined as

\hat{A}_t^{\mathrm{GAE}(\gamma,\lambda)}
= (1-\lambda)\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\lambda^{k-1}\hat{A}_t^{(k)}.

Substituting the k-step estimators into this expression yields

\hat{A}_t^{\mathrm{GAE}(\gamma,\lambda)}
= (1-\lambda)\left(
\hat{A}_t^{(1)} + \lambda \hat{A}_t^{(2)} + \lambda^2 \hat{A}_t^{(3)} + \cdots
\right).

Expanding each term in TD residual form gives

\hat{A}_t^{\mathrm{GAE}(\gamma,\lambda)}
= (1-\lambda)\left(
\delta_t
+ \lambda(\delta_t + \gamma \delta_{t+1})
+ \lambda^2(\delta_t + \gamma \delta_{t+1} + \gamma^2 \delta_{t+2})
+ \cdots
\right).

We then collect coefficients of each residual \delta_{t+l}. For a fixed l, its coefficient is

(1-\lambda)\left(
\lambda^l \gamma^l + \lambda^{l+1}\gamma^l + \lambda^{l+2}\gamma^l + \cdots
\right).

Factoring out (\gamma\lambda)^l gives

(1-\lambda)(\gamma\lambda)^l(1 + \lambda + \lambda^2 + \cdots).

Using the geometric series identity

1 + \lambda + \lambda^2 + \cdots = \frac{1}{1-\lambda},
\qquad \text{for } 0 \le \lambda < 1,

the (1-\lambda) term cancels, leaving

(\gamma\lambda)^l

as the coefficient on \delta_{t+l}. Therefore, GAE simplifies to the compact form

\hat{A}_t^{\mathrm{GAE}(\gamma,\lambda)}
= \sum_{l=0}^{\infty} (\gamma\lambda)^l \delta_{t+l}.

In practice, PPO does not operate on infinite trajectories. Instead, it collects trajectory segments of finite length T, so the estimator is truncated at the end of the rollout:

\hat{A}_t = \sum_{l=0}^{T-t-1} (\gamma\lambda)^l \delta_{t+l}.

This final expression makes clear that GAE is not a separate idea from temporal-difference learning, but rather a structured generalization of it. The one-step TD residual remains the atomic unit, while \lambda controls how far future residuals are allowed to influence the estimate. When \lambda is small, the estimator stays close to low-variance bootstrapping; when \lambda approaches 1, it moves toward longer-horizon returns with lower bias but higher variance.
This derivation also clarifies why GAE is so important for PPO. The clipped surrogate objective does not operate directly on rewards; it operates on advantage estimates. If those estimates are excessively noisy, the probability ratio may be pushed in unstable directions even when clipping is present. GAE provides a smoother and more reliable policy gradient signal, making it possible for PPO to reuse the same batch over multiple optimization epochs without immediately overreacting to high-variance returns. In this sense, the clipped objective constrains how far the policy may move, while GAE improves the quality of the signal telling it which direction to move.

title: LLM Alignment Series: Proximal Policy Optimization
text:
3 PPO Training Pipeline
Having derived Generalized Advantage Estimation, we now have the advantage signal that PPO uses to guide policy improvement. These estimates enter directly into the clipped surrogate objective and provide a practical balance between bias and variance during optimization. We are therefore ready to move from the construction of the learning signal to the structure of the algorithm itself. The next section examines the PPO training pipeline, where policy loss, value regression, and entropy regularization are combined within an iterative rollout-and-update procedure.

3.1 The Full PPO Objective
In architectures where the policy and value function share neural network parameters, training must optimize both components through a single composite objective. This shared representation creates an important design constraint: the network must learn features that are simultaneously useful for action selection and for estimating future returns. PPO addresses this by combining three distinct terms into one objective function.
The full objective is written as

L_t^{CLIP+VF+S}(\theta)
=
\hat{\mathbb{E}}_t
\left[
L_t^{CLIP}(\theta)
- c_1 L_t^{VF}(\theta)
+ c_2 S[\pi_\theta](s_t)
\right].

The first term, L_t^{CLIP}(\theta), is the clipped surrogate objective. This is the core policy optimization term. Using the advantage estimates produced by GAE, it increases the probability of actions that performed better than expected and decreases the probability of actions that performed worse than expected. At the same time, the clipping mechanism limits how far the policy is allowed to move in a single update, thereby preventing the unstable jumps that can arise in unconstrained policy gradient methods.
The second term, L_t^{VF}(\theta), is the value function loss. Reliable policy updates depend on reliable advantage estimates, and reliable advantage estimates in turn depend on an accurate value baseline. For this reason, PPO trains the critic alongside the actor using a squared-error objective of the form

L_t^{VF}(\theta)
=
\left(
V_\theta(s_t) - V_t^{\mathrm{targ}}
\right)^2.

Here, V_t^{\mathrm{targ}} is a target return constructed from the observed trajectory. Because PPO is written as a maximization objective, the value loss appears with a negative sign. Maximizing the overall objective therefore corresponds to minimizing the critic’s prediction error while simultaneously improving the policy.
The third term, S[\pi_\theta](s_t), is an entropy bonus. Entropy measures the uncertainty, or spread, of the policy’s action distribution. Including this term encourages the policy to remain sufficiently stochastic during training rather than collapsing too early to a narrow or deterministic strategy. This plays an important regularizing role: without an entropy bonus, the policy may prematurely overcommit to actions that happened to receive favorable advantage estimates early in training, reducing exploration and potentially trapping learning in a suboptimal regime.
Taken together, these three components define the optimization structure of PPO. The clipped policy term drives improvement, the value loss stabilizes the advantage estimates that guide that improvement, and the entropy bonus preserves exploration while training remains underway. When the actor and critic share parameters, this unified objective also allows all gradients to be propagated through the shared network in a single backward pass. As a result, the lower layers learn state representations that are shaped simultaneously by policy improvement, value estimation, and exploration pressure.
The coefficients c_1 and c_2 determine the relative influence of the value loss and entropy bonus. In practice, these hyperparameters are essential: if the critic term is weighted too heavily, value fitting can dominate policy learning, while an excessively large entropy coefficient can prevent the policy from becoming sufficiently decisive. PPO therefore depends not only on clipping, but also on a careful balance among these three gradient signals.


3.2 Rollout Buffer vs. Replay Buffer
To understand why Proximal Policy Optimization does not rely on a traditional replay buffer, it is necessary to contrast its mathematical structure with that of explicitly off-policy algorithms. In methods such as Deep Q-Networks (DQN) and Soft Actor-Critic (SAC), the agent maintains a large and persistent buffer of past interactions. Because these methods are derived from Bellman-style updates that target optimal future behavior rather than the precise behavior policy that generated the data, they can safely reuse trajectories collected many iterations earlier.
PPO operates under a different regime. Its update is built around the probability ratio

r_t(\theta) = \frac{\pi_\theta(a_t \mid s_t)}{\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}(a_t \mid s_t)},

which corrects for the mismatch between the current policy and the policy that generated the sampled trajectories. This is an importance-sampling correction, but it is only reliable when the two policies remain close. PPO’s clipped objective explicitly enforces this locality by constraining the effective update region to ratios near 1, typically within the interval

[1-\epsilon,\, 1+\epsilon].

This immediately limits how off-policy the training data can be. If PPO were to draw trajectories from a permanent replay buffer containing samples generated many policy iterations earlier, the divergence between \pi_\theta and \pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}} could become very large. In that case, the probability ratio would frequently fall far outside the clipping interval, and the clipped surrogate objective would saturate on a large fraction of the data. Once this happens, the gradient signal becomes weak or uninformative, and optimization becomes ineffective. PPO can therefore tolerate only modest policy drift between data collection and update. Its data is not fully on-policy in a strict mathematical sense, since multiple epochs are performed on the same batch, but it is only mildly off-policy within a tightly controlled window.
This theoretical constraint determines the engineering design of PPO. Instead of a persistent replay buffer, PPO uses a transient rollout buffer whose contents are valid only for a short optimization cycle. As described in the original algorithm, training proceeds through an alternating loop of rollout collection, advantage computation, and limited reuse.
The process begins with parallel data collection. A set of N actors runs the current policy in the environment for T timesteps each, producing a batch of NT transitions. These transitions contain states, actions, rewards, old action probabilities, and value predictions under the current policy at the time of sampling.
Once this rollout has been collected, interaction with the environment pauses and the algorithm computes training targets. Using the sampled rewards together with the critic’s value estimates, PPO computes temporal-difference residuals and then applies Generalized Advantage Estimation to obtain the advantage estimates \hat{A}_t. At the same time, target values V_t^{\mathrm{targ}} are formed for critic regression.
The algorithm then enters the optimization phase. The collected batch is shuffled, divided into minibatches, and reused for K epochs of stochastic gradient optimization. During this stage, PPO maximizes the composite objective consisting of the clipped policy term, the value function term, and the entropy bonus. The key point is that the batch may be reused several times, but only for a limited number of epochs. This limited reuse is precisely what PPO’s importance-sampling correction can tolerate: enough to improve sample efficiency, but not enough to let the current policy drift arbitrarily far from the sampling policy.
After these K epochs, the rollout buffer is discarded. The current parameters become the new reference policy for the next iteration, and a fresh batch of trajectories must be collected from the environment. In this sense, PPO follows a short-horizon data lifecycle: collect, estimate, optimize, discard, and recollect.
This design is sometimes described as a compromise between strictly on-policy and fully off-policy reinforcement learning. PPO improves upon vanilla on-policy methods by extracting multiple gradient steps from each batch, but it stops far short of the replay-based regime used by DQN or SAC. The clipped objective makes this compromise possible, but it also imposes its central limitation: data may be reused only while it still reflects a policy close to the current one. For that reason, PPO does not maintain a replay buffer in the conventional sense. Its rollout buffer is intentionally ephemeral, because the usefulness of the data decays as soon as the policy moves too far from the one that generated it.

title: LLM Alignment Series: Proximal Policy Optimization
section: 4 PPO and the Computational Cost of RLHF
text:
4 PPO and the Computational Cost of RLHF
The main bottleneck in applying reinforcement learning to large language models is very different from the bottleneck in classical control problems. In simulated robotics or game environments, collecting trajectories is usually relatively cheap. The environment can be stepped forward quickly, and the main cost often lies in optimization. In language modeling, however, the rollout process is the generation process itself. Producing a response requires autoregressive decoding, where tokens are generated one by one through repeated forward passes of a large transformer. For modern language models, this is expensive in both latency and hardware utilization.
This difference has an important consequence for RLHF. In a strictly on-policy method, each batch of generated samples would be used once for a single gradient update and then discarded. That would make training highly inefficient, since most of the wall-clock time would be spent generating new text rather than improving the model from existing data. In other words, the cost of sampling would dominate the cost of learning.
PPO helps with this problem because it allows limited sample reuse. By using the probability ratio r_t(\theta) together with the clipped surrogate objective, PPO can perform several optimization epochs on the same batch of generated sequences, as long as the policy does not move too far from the one that produced the data. The hyperparameter K controls how many passes are made over the rollout batch before a new batch must be generated.
This changes the training cost structure in an important way. Instead of paying the full cost of autoregressive generation for every gradient step, PPO spreads that cost across multiple updates. During these optimization epochs, the model still has to recompute log-probabilities under the current policy in order to evaluate r_t(\theta). But because the token sequences are already fixed in the rollout buffer, these computations no longer require sequential sampling. They can be evaluated in parallel over the full sequence with causal masking, which is much cheaper than generating tokens one at a time.
For this reason, PPO is not only a stable policy optimization method in theory. In RLHF, it is also a practical way to make reinforcement learning feasible for large language models. The clipped objective does more than stabilize updates: it also makes limited sample reuse possible, which significantly reduces the cost of training.

title: LLM Alignment Series: Proximal Policy Optimization
text:
5 Beyond PPO
Although PPO reduces the cost of alignment by reusing samples across several optimization epochs, it still depends on an expensive online training loop. In large language model alignment, PPO often requires several model components to remain active during training, including the current policy, a value function, a reference model, and a reward model. Each iteration also requires a fresh rollout buffer built through autoregressive generation. As models continue to grow, both the memory requirements of this setup and the latency of live sampling become increasingly difficult to manage.
This is the context in which methods such as Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) (Rafailov et al. 2024) emerged. Instead of treating alignment as an online reinforcement learning problem, DPO reformulates it as direct optimization on static preference data. In standard RLHF, the objective is usually written as reward maximization regularized by a KL constraint that keeps the policy close to a reference model. DPO shows that, under a preference model such as Bradley-Terry, this optimization problem can be rewritten so that the reward is represented implicitly through the policy and reference log-probabilities:

r(x,y) = \beta \log \frac{\pi_\theta(y \mid x)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y \mid x)}.

This removes the need to train a separate reward model and avoids the full PPO pipeline of online sampling, reward fitting, value estimation, and policy optimization. Instead, the policy is trained directly on chosen-versus-rejected response pairs, with the objective encouraging higher relative probability on preferred outputs.
Kahneman-Tversky Optimization (KTO) (Ethayarajh et al. 2024) pushes this simplification further by relaxing the paired-data requirement used in DPO. DPO assumes that, for each prompt, one has both a preferred and a dispreferred response. KTO instead works with unpaired binary feedback, where a sample is labeled only as desirable or undesirable. This makes the method easier to apply when full preference pairs are difficult to collect or curate. Like DPO, KTO avoids online rollout generation and operates directly on a fixed dataset with a deterministic objective.
DPO and KTO are part of a broader move toward simpler preference-based alignment objectives. IPO, or Identity Preference Optimization (Azar et al. 2023), revisits the DPO-style formulation and modifies the objective in a way intended to improve optimization behavior. ORPO, or Odds Ratio Preference Optimization (Hong et al. 2024), combines supervised fine-tuning and preference optimization into a single stage, which makes the training pipeline simpler. SimPO, or Simple Preference Optimization (Meng et al. 2024), further reduces the dependence on an explicit reference model while keeping the basic preference-learning structure. More recently, GRPO, or Group Relative Policy Optimization (Shao et al. 2024), has attracted attention in settings where relative comparisons across multiple candidates are more natural than scalar reward modeling, especially in reasoning-focused training.
These methods are better understood not as rejections of PPO, but as simpler reformulations of the same alignment goal. All of them aim to move the model distribution toward outputs preferred by humans while limiting excessive drift from a reference behavior. The main difference is procedural. PPO approaches this through online reinforcement learning with controlled policy updates. DPO, KTO, IPO, ORPO, SimPO, and related methods instead replace much of that machinery with offline or more direct objectives defined on preference data.
As alignment workloads scale to larger models, these methods become increasingly attractive because they preserve the core preference-learning structure of RLHF while avoiding much of the overhead associated with live sampling, critic training, and reward-model optimization. In that sense, they extend the same line of work: not by rejecting PPO, but by asking whether a similar alignment objective can be reached with a cheaper and simpler training procedure.

title: Agentic AI Series: SWE-agent and Autonomous Software Engineering
Agentic AI Series: SWE-agent and Autonomous Software Engineering
text:
1 Introduction
Recent advances in large language models have substantially improved code generation, yet repository-level software engineering remains far more difficult than short-form code synthesis. Real bug fixing requires long-horizon interaction with a codebase: the model must identify relevant files, inspect local context, propose edits, execute commands, and revise its strategy based on runtime feedback.
SWE-agent (Yang et al. 2024)addresses this gap by formulating software engineering as an interactive decision-making problem rather than a one-shot generation task. Instead of directly predicting a patch from an issue description, the system allows a language model to interact with a repository through a structured Agent–Computer Interface (ACI). At each step, the agent observes the current environment state, selects an action such as search, file viewing, editing, or command execution, and then conditions subsequent reasoning on the resulting feedback.
This design is important because it shifts the focus from model-only reasoning to interface-mediated problem solving. The central claim of SWE-agent is that the effectiveness of a coding agent depends not only on the underlying language model, but also on how the action space and feedback channel are organized. By simplifying repository navigation, constraining editing operations, and exposing concise execution feedback, the ACI makes long-horizon software engineering tasks more tractable for the model.
From a broader perspective, SWE-agent marks an early transition from static code generation to autonomous software engineering agents. It shows that real-world code repair is better understood as sequential interaction over program states than as single-step text completion. This perspective has shaped much of the subsequent work on coding agents, including systems that incorporate stronger search, verifier modules, and reinforcement learning-based optimization.
SWE-agent begins by changing the problem formulation. The goal is not to ask a language model to directly produce a patch from an issue description. Instead, the model is treated as an interactive agent that observes the environment, selects an action, receives feedback, and continues to the next step.
Under this view, repository-level bug fixing is no longer framed as a one-shot mapping from issue text to patch. It is instead modeled as an iterative workflow in which the agent searches the repository, opens relevant files, localizes the faulty code region, applies edits, executes tests or scripts, and revises its behavior in response to the resulting feedback. This reformulation is important because it shifts the task from static code generation to sequential decision-making over program states.
At a high level, the architecture is simple. SWE-agent consists of a language model, an Agent–Computer Interface (ACI), and an execution environment. The language model is responsible for reasoning and action selection. The ACI packages computer functionality into an interface that is easier for the model to use effectively. The execution environment remains a real software environment built on top of the Linux shell, repository files, and testing infrastructure. The central methodological choice is therefore not to train a new model, but to keep the model fixed and improve the interaction layer.

title: Agentic AI Series: SWE-agent and Autonomous Software Engineering
text:
2 ACI Components
The paper organizes the ACI into four components: search and navigation, file viewing, file editing, and context management.

2.1 Search and Navigation
The first subproblem is repository localization. Before the agent can modify code, it must identify which files and positions are relevant to the issue. To support this process, SWE-agent introduces dedicated commands such as find_file, search_file, and search_dir.
These commands do not expose raw shell output in full. Instead, they return summarized search results. When a query is too broad, the interface prompts the agent to refine it rather than flooding the context with low-value matches. This design turns repository search into a controlled localization procedure rather than unrestricted shell exploration.


2.2 File Viewer
Once a relevant file has been identified, the agent does not simply print the entire file. SWE-agent instead provides an interactive file viewer with commands such as open, scroll_up, scroll_down, and goto.
The viewer displays a bounded window of lines together with the full file path, total line count, omitted regions above and below the current window, and explicit line numbers. This makes local inspection possible without overwhelming the context window with an entire file dump.


2.3 File Editor
The file editor is one of the most important components of the system. Rather than requiring the model to compose fragile shell editing commands, SWE-agent provides a dedicated edit command that takes a start line, an end line, and replacement text.
This abstraction compresses multi-line editing into a single structured action. After the edit is applied, the viewer immediately shows the updated content so that the model can verify the effect of its modification.
This design matters because shell-native editing is a poor match for language models. Whole-file rewrites are cumbersome, sed-style edits are brittle, and silent modifications make it difficult for the model to maintain an accurate internal state.


2.4 Context Management
Context management is easy to overlook, but it is central to the method. SWE-agent provides the model with instructions, command documentation, and demonstrations. At each step, the model is expected to emit both a thought and an action. Malformed generations trigger an explicit error response and the model is asked to retry. Commands that succeed without producing output are reported as such, rather than leaving the model to infer what happened.
Old observations are also compressed into short placeholders. This preserves the interaction structure while preventing stale outputs from dominating the working context. In effect, the system actively manages context rather than passively accumulating it.

title: Agentic AI Series: SWE-agent and Autonomous Software Engineering
section: 3 Execution Loop versus Verifier and Test-Time Search
text:
3 Execution Loop versus Verifier and Test-Time Search
The execution loop follows a standard ReAct-style pattern (Yao et al. 2023). At each step, the agent generates a thought and a command, executes that command in the environment, receives feedback, and conditions the next round of reasoning on the resulting observation.
Operationally, the loop can be described in plain terms. The agent first reads the issue, then determines the next useful action, executes that action, inspects the returned feedback, and continues until it is ready to submit a patch.
This is not a planner–executor decomposition and not a multi-agent design. It is a single-agent closed loop over repository state.
Both execution feedback and verifier-based methods use runtime signals to improve performance, but they operate at different levels of the decision process. The central distinction is the following. In SWE-agent, execution feedback functions as an online observation signal within the agent loop. By contrast, a verifier acts more like an external evaluator, while test-time search acts as an additional strategy for exploring alternative solution paths.

3.1 Execution Feedback as Online Environment Observation
The paper defines SWE-agent as an interactive system in which, at each step, the model generates a thought and a command, then incorporates the feedback from command execution into the next decision.
In abstract form, the interaction loop can be written as

\text{think} \;\rightarrow\; \text{act} \;\rightarrow\; \text{observe} \;\rightarrow\; \text{think again}.

Here, execution feedback is not limited to test outcomes. It includes summarized search results, outputs from the file viewer, updated file contents after editing, and the outputs of shell commands, tests, or reproduction scripts. All of these are forms of environment feedback consumed by the agent during the trajectory.
For this reason, execution feedback in SWE-agent should not be understood as a final judgment. It is the observation stream on which the agent conditions each subsequent action.


3.2 A Verifier as an Evaluation Module
A verifier serves a different role. At a high level, a verifier evaluates whether a candidate patch, answer, or trajectory is credible. It may score candidates, rank multiple outputs, or provide a pass/fail or confidence signal at some stage of inference.
This is different from the role played by execution feedback in SWE-agent. The feedback collected by SWE-agent is not introduced as an independent judge of global solution quality. Instead, it consists of first-hand signals from the environment: which files were returned by a search query, what a particular code region looks like, how the file changed after an edit, or what error message was produced by a script. These signals are used primarily to determine the next action, not to assign a final score to the overall solution.
In this sense, a verifier is closer to an evaluation component, whereas execution feedback is closer to an interaction component.


3.3 Test-Time Search as Multi-Path Exploration
The term test-time search usually refers to methods that allocate additional computation to explore multiple candidate reasoning or action paths. This may involve branching, backtracking, reranking, or systematic exploration of several possible trajectories.
SWE-agent does not primarily operate in this way. Its core framework is a ReAct-style single-trajectory interaction loop rather than a tree-search procedure or a multi-branch rollout system. The agent repeatedly searches, edits, executes, and updates its state, but these operations occur within one evolving trajectory.
This difference is important. Test-time search expands the breadth of the search over candidate solutions. Execution feedback, by contrast, improves the adaptability of the current trajectory. The former asks whether additional solution paths should be explored. The latter asks how the present trajectory should be adjusted in light of new observations.


3.4 Localization and Recovery
The paper decomposes the software engineering task into three core subtasks: localization, editing, and testing.
Within this decomposition, the role of execution feedback is not merely to verify whether the final answer is correct. Its more immediate function is to help the agent narrow an issue description to relevant files and lines, inspect the post-edit state of the code, and decide whether to continue editing, run another search, or move to a different location after failure.
This is a substantial difference from the role of a verifier. A verifier typically appears later in the pipeline and asks whether a candidate result is good. Execution feedback in SWE-agent appears earlier and more frequently. It asks what the agent should inspect next, where it should navigate, and how it should revise its current plan.


3.5 Guardrails as a Boundary Case
Some mechanisms in SWE-agent lie conceptually between online feedback and verification. The clearest example is the combination of structured editing and linting. When an edit introduces major errors, the system does not simply accept the modification. Instead, it surfaces the error information and asks the agent to retry. The paper explicitly presents this mechanism as part of the guardrail design used to improve robustness.
Even so, this is still not equivalent to a typical verifier. The linting mechanism does not assign a global quality score to the entire patch. It operates locally at the moment an edit is attempted, blocks invalid state transitions, and returns information directly into the active interaction loop. Its function is therefore better described as online feedback plus recovery rather than a separate global evaluator.
The distinction can be stated compactly. In SWE-agent, execution feedback is the online observation signal obtained at each step of interaction with the environment. It drives subsequent search, localization, editing, and recovery decisions. A verifier is better understood as an external evaluator of candidate outputs. Test-time search is best understood as an additional strategy for exploring multiple solution paths.
In short, execution feedback addresses the question of what to do next. A verifier addresses the question of whether the current result is good. Test-time search addresses the question of whether more candidate paths should be explored.

title: Agentic AI Series: SWE-agent and Autonomous Software Engineering
text:
4 Context Management in Long-Horizon Tasks
SWE-agent’s context management for long-horizon software engineering can be understood as a deliberately minimalist memory design: it preserves the trajectory while discarding much of the payload. Rather than building an increasingly elaborate memory system, it tightly controls which parts of the interaction history are allowed to consume the current context budget. This role is handled by a history_processor, which reconstructs the literal history shown to the model at each step from the full interaction trace.
Two mechanisms are central. First, old observations are automatically collapsed. SWE-agent keeps the order and structure of prior interactions, but replaces the detailed content of older observations with a one-line placeholder such as “Old output omitted (101 lines).” This reduces token usage and removes stale or duplicated information, including earlier directory listings, previous file contents, and outdated command outputs. Second, the system applies strict state tracking and de-noising. Malformed responses trigger format errors, repeated malformed outputs can terminate the episode, and invalid interaction fragments are removed from retained history once a valid response is produced. These choices are empirically grounded: in the paper’s hyperparameter sweep, a 100-line window with only the last five observations outperformed the same window size with full history for GPT-4 Turbo.
Compared with retrieval-augmented memory, SWE-agent follows the opposite design philosophy. Systems such as MemGPT (Packer et al. 2023) or Reflexion (Shinn et al. 2023) attempt to preserve and later recover past information through hierarchical storage or episodic reuse. SWE-agent instead assumes that much of the past should be forgotten. It does not construct a revisitable long-term memory store, nor does it actively retrieve potentially useful fragments from earlier trajectories. Instead, it keeps only recent and locally relevant observations in high resolution and compresses the rest. The key asymmetry is therefore the following: retrieval-augmented memory addresses the problem that useful information may lie beyond the immediate context window, whereas SWE-agent addresses the problem that long interaction histories are not only large but also noisy. In repository-level coding, stale shell outputs, superseded file snippets, and obsolete error messages are often less like knowledge and more like attention liabilities.
The contrast with multi-agent collaboration is equally important. Multi-agent systems typically mitigate long-horizon difficulty by distributing cognition across roles, communication channels, and coordination structures. SWE-agent does not do this. It does not decompose repository search, editing, and verification across multiple agents, nor does it build shared memory across roles. Instead, it assumes a single agent and tries to keep that agent’s trajectory clean, executable, and format-controlled. The trade-off is clear: multi-agent systems exchange additional structure for stronger decomposition, whereas SWE-agent exchanges representational richness for lower coordination cost and tighter local control.
This design is especially effective when viewed through the lens of long-context attention and compute allocation. SWE-agent does not attempt to improve the model’s ability to remember distant tokens. It simply removes many distant tokens from high-resolution context. Once old observations are collapsed, the model no longer needs to allocate attention across obsolete shell outputs, previous file contents, or earlier directory states. The combination of a 100-line viewing window and only the most recent observations concentrates computation on the current program state rather than the full interaction archive. The cost, however, is that if genuinely important early details become relevant again, the system has no sophisticated recall mechanism; it must re-search the repository, reopen files, or rerun commands to recover them.
From a broader perspective, SWE-agent makes a clear efficiency trade-off. It gives up long-range revisitation, explicit experience accumulation, and collaborative problem decomposition in exchange for lower context entropy, lower coordination overhead, and a more stable single-trajectory allocation of test-time compute. Its broader theoretical contribution is to show that long-horizon memory management does not always require stronger retention and retrieval. It can also emerge from stricter forgetting. Importantly, this forgetting is structured rather than arbitrary: SWE-agent preserves the causal skeleton of the interaction while compressing away much of the obsolete payload. In that sense, its contribution is less a general-purpose memory architecture than a state-controlled form of context compression.

title: Agentic AI Series: SWE-agent and Autonomous Software Engineering
text:
5 Why This Framework Works
The effectiveness of SWE-agent does not come primarily from the scale of the language model, but from the structure of the interaction interface. The ACI design introduces several constraints and abstractions that significantly improve the agent’s ability to solve long-horizon software engineering tasks. The paper evaluates these design choices through ablation experiments and qualitative analysis.
At a high level, the improvements arise from three mechanisms: summarized search results that improve repository localization, a windowed file viewer that stabilizes context usage, and a structured editing interface with syntax-aware validation.

5.1 Summarized Search Improves Repository Localization
A naive approach to repository exploration would allow the language model to run arbitrary shell commands such as grep or ls and then return the full output. In practice, this often produces extremely long outputs that overwhelm the model’s context window.
SWE-agent instead returns summarized search results. Rather than printing every matching line, the system compresses the results and provides a concise overview. When the number of matches is large, the interface explicitly instructs the agent to refine its query.
This change has two important effects. First, it reduces context noise. Only the most relevant signals are preserved in the prompt, which allows the model to maintain a coherent working memory. Second, it encourages a more structured search strategy. The agent must iteratively narrow the search space rather than relying on brute-force output inspection. In repository-scale codebases, this dramatically improves the reliability of code localization.


5.2 The 100-Line Viewer Stabilizes Context Usage
Another difficulty in repository-level tasks is that source files are often hundreds or thousands of lines long. A naive interface that simply prints the entire file introduces two problems.
The first problem is context overflow. Large files can easily exceed the available context window, causing the model to lose important information from earlier steps. The second problem is cognitive overload. When a full file is displayed, the model must reason about a large amount of irrelevant code.
SWE-agent addresses this issue with a windowed viewer that displays at most 100 lines at a time. The viewer also provides metadata such as the total number of lines in the file, the current window position, and explicit line numbers.
This design introduces a form of spatial locality. The agent inspects code in bounded segments and navigates through the file using scrolling commands. As a result, the model can focus on local reasoning without being overwhelmed by the full file content. In long debugging trajectories, this significantly stabilizes the working context.


5.3 Structured Editing with Linter Feedback
Editing code through a raw shell interface is surprisingly fragile for language models. Multi-line edits using tools such as sed or awk are difficult to compose correctly, and small syntax mistakes can silently corrupt the file.
SWE-agent replaces this with a structured edit command that explicitly specifies the starting line, the ending line, and the replacement content. This abstraction transforms code modification into a single well-defined action. After the edit is applied, the viewer immediately shows the updated region so the model can verify the result.
In addition, the interface integrates a linter that detects syntax errors introduced by the edit. When an edit fails the syntax check, the system discards the modification and reports the error back to the agent. This feedback loop prevents invalid edits from propagating through later steps and allows the model to correct mistakes immediately.


5.4 Why These Changes Matter
Taken together, these design choices reshape the reasoning process of the language model. Instead of interacting with an unconstrained shell environment, the agent operates within a structured action space where navigation, inspection, editing, and feedback are carefully controlled.
The summarized search interface improves repository localization. The windowed viewer preserves context stability during long trajectories. The structured editing interface reduces error-prone operations and introduces immediate syntactic verification.
From a systems perspective, these components transform the coding task into a sequence of small, well-defined decisions. This structured interaction loop allows the language model to allocate its reasoning capacity to program understanding rather than low-level command construction.

title: Agentic AI Series: SWE-agent and Autonomous Software Engineering
text:
6 Conclusion
The key design contribution of SWE-agent lies in the introduction of an Agent–Computer Interface (ACI), a structured command environment that mediates all interactions between the language model and the software repository. Instead of allowing unrestricted natural-language reasoning or arbitrary tool invocation, the ACI constrains the action space to a set of well-defined operations such as file viewing, code editing, and test execution. This design has two important consequences.
First, it converts the open-ended reasoning process of the language model into a controlled interaction loop where each step produces observable feedback. This feedback includes syntactic signals from linters, runtime signals from test execution, and repository state updates. Such signals act as implicit verification mechanisms that guide the model toward correct solutions.
Second, the structured interface induces a form of test-time search. The agent repeatedly proposes candidate modifications, evaluates them through environment feedback, and revises its strategy accordingly. In this sense, SWE-agent shifts the computational burden from static inference toward interactive exploration during execution.
This perspective is closely related to the emerging notion of test-time compute, where additional reasoning steps, tool calls, and environment interactions are used to improve solution quality without modifying the underlying model parameters. Instead of relying solely on model scaling, SWE-agent demonstrates that carefully designed execution environments can significantly extend the practical capabilities of language models in complex engineering tasks.
The broader significance of this framework is that it establishes a concrete bridge between language models and software engineering environments. By structuring interaction through the ACI and leveraging execution feedback as a verification signal, SWE-agent provides an early prototype of autonomous coding agents capable of performing long-horizon debugging tasks in real repositories. Subsequent research on autonomous software agents—including verifier-based coding systems and reinforcement learning–based training environments—can be understood as extensions of this foundational interaction paradigm.

title: LLM Alignment Series: Trust Region Policy Optimization
text:
2026-03-06
Trust Region Policy Optimization (TRPO) (Schulman, Levine, et al. 2017) is a policy-based reinforcement learning method that shares the same fundamental objective function as standard policy gradient algorithms: maximizing the expected value J(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_S[V_\pi(S)].
As shown by the Policy Gradient Theorem (see my previous post LLM Alignment Series: The Policy Gradient Theorem), this objective can be optimized by estimating the gradient of J(\theta) with respect to the policy parameters. Importantly, TRPO does not change this objective; instead, it modifies how the policy update is performed by constraining how far the new policy can move from the old one. While standard policy gradient algorithms rely on stochastic gradient ascent to improve the policy, TRPO utilizes a trust-region algorithm. This approach ensures more stable and reliable updates by constraining how much the policy can change in a single step, helping to prevent the performance collapses often seen with traditional gradient methods. In the next post LLM Alignment Series: Proximal Policy Optimization, we will see how Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) builds on the same idea but replaces the trust-region constraint with a simpler clipped objective (Schulman, Wolski, et al. 2017) that is easier to implement in modern deep learning pipelines.

title: LLM Alignment Series: Trust Region Policy Optimization
text:
1 Trust Region Optimization
At its core, Trust Region optimization is a strategy for safely navigating complex, non-linear objective functions f(x) by relying on bounded local approximations. Instead of picking a direction and then guessing a step size like standard line search methods, trust region methods first define a safe maximum step distance, and then find the optimal update within that strict boundary.
The algorithm proceeds in three main phases:

The Local Approximation
At the current parameter state x_k, we construct a simplified local model of the landscape, typically a second-order Taylor expansion denoted as m_k(p), where p is the proposed step vector. We mathematically “trust” this approximation is accurate only within a specific radius, \Delta_k.
The Constrained Subproblem
We find the optimal step p by minimizing the local model subject to the trust-region boundary constraint:
Minimize: m_k(p)
Subject to: \|p\| \le \Delta_k
The Dynamic Evaluation
Before officially updating the parameters, we measure how well our local model predicted the actual landscape. We calculate the agreement ratio \rho_k, which compares the actual reduction in the true objective function to the predicted reduction from our simplified model:
\rho_k = \frac{f(x_k) - f(x_k + p_k)}{m_k(0) - m_k(p_k)}

Based on \rho_k, the algorithm dynamically adjusts. If \rho_k is close to 1, the model is highly accurate; the step is accepted, and the trust region \Delta_k is expanded for faster optimization. If \rho_k is negative, the model was wrong and the step actually made things worse; the step is rejected, the trust region is shrunk, and the algorithm tries again within a tighter, safer boundary. This feedback loop guarantees stable, monotonic improvement even in highly unpredictable loss landscapes.

title: LLM Alignment Series: Trust Region Policy Optimization
text:
2 Trust Region Policy Optimization (TRPO)

2.1 The Surrogate Objective
Policy Gradient Theorem proves that the gradient of the state distribution does not affect the policy gradient at the current parameters \theta, it saves us from modeling the environment’s transition dynamics. This shortcut only holds true for the exact gradient at the current \theta. This is exactly why TRPO cannot just use J(\theta) and must rely on the surrogate objective L(\theta).
Instead of directly maximizing the expected return J(\theta), TRPO optimizes a surrogate objective function. Let \theta_{old} be the parameters of the current policy and \theta be the parameters of the proposed new policy. TRPO seeks to maximize the following expected advantage:
L(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{s, a \sim \pi_{\theta_{old}}} \left[ \frac{\pi_{\theta}(a|s)}{\pi_{\theta_{old}}(a|s)} A_{\theta_{old}}(s, a) \right]
In this equation, A_{\theta_{old}}(s, a) is the advantage function, which measures how much better a specific action is compared to the average baseline action in a given state. The ratio \frac{\pi_{\theta}(a|s)}{\pi_{\theta_{old}}(a|s)} tracks how the probability of taking that action changes under the new policy.
It was proved that the true objective J(\theta) is mathematically guaranteed to improve as long as L(\theta) improves and the Kullback-Leibler divergence between the old and new policies is strictly penalized (Schulman, Levine, et al. 2017) . By enforcing a hard constraint on this KL divergence, TRPO traps the optimization step inside a safe, narrow boundary where L(\theta) remains a valid and reliable proxy for J(\theta).


2.2 The KL Divergence Constraint
To prevent the catastrophic updates mentioned earlier, TRPO restricts the change in the policy using Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence, a mathematical statistic that measures how one probability distribution differs from a second, reference probability distribution.
Rather than just adding a penalty to the objective function, TRPO enforces a hard constraint on the average KL divergence over the state space. The formal constrained optimization problem is written as:
Maximize:
L(\theta) \tag{1}
Subject to:
\mathbb{E}_{s \sim \rho_{\theta_{old}}} \left[ D_{KL}(\pi_{\theta_{old}}(\cdot|s) \parallel \pi_{\theta}(\cdot|s)) \right] \le \delta
The parameter \delta is a predefined, small scalar value that defines the maximum allowed KL divergence. This creates the “trust region” around the current policy. By enforcing this boundary, the algorithm mathematically guarantees that the new policy \pi_{\theta} will not diverge significantly from \pi_{\theta_{old}} for any given state. Because the policy is only allowed to change within this safe, trusted region, TRPO maintains stable and theoretically guaranteed monotonic improvement during the learning process.


2.3 Local Approximation using Taylor Expansion
Let the change in policy parameters be \Delta \theta = \theta - \theta_{old}.
First, we approximate the objective function L(\theta) using a first-order Taylor expansion around \theta_{old}:
L(\theta) \approx L(\theta_{old}) + g^T \Delta \theta
Here, g is the policy gradient evaluated at \theta_{old}:
g = \nabla_{\theta} L(\theta)|_{\theta=\theta_{old}}
Second, we approximate the KL divergence constraint using a second-order Taylor expansion. The zeroth and first-order terms of the KL divergence between identical distributions are zero, leaving only the second-order term. The detailed proof is provided in Section 4.
\bar{D}_{KL}(\theta_{old}, \theta) \approx \frac{1}{2} \Delta \theta^T H \Delta \theta
Here, H is the Hessian matrix of the KL divergence. In the context of probability distributions, this Hessian is equivalent to the Fisher Information Matrix (FIM), as shown in Section 5.
\bar{D}_{KL}(\theta_{old}, \theta) is a shorthand convention used heavily in the actual TRPO paper to make the equations readable. The bar on top denotes a mean or expectation. It specifically represents the average KL divergence over all the states actually sampled in the rollout buffer. Mathematically, it is defined as: \bar{D}_{KL}(\theta_{old}, \theta) = \mathbb{E}_{s \sim \rho_{\theta_{old}}} \left[ D_{KL}(\pi_{\theta_{old}}(\cdot|s) \parallel \pi_\theta(\cdot|s)) \right] D_{KL}(\pi_{\theta_{old}}(\cdot|s) \parallel \pi_\theta(\cdot|s)) is the exact, formal application of that concept to our policy networks. It represents the KL divergence between the old policy and the new policy at one single, specific state s.
By substituting these approximations back into the original TRPO formulation Equation 1, the problem simplifies into a quadratic program:
Maximize:
g^T \Delta \theta
Subject to:
\frac{1}{2} \Delta \theta^T H \Delta \theta \le \delta
To find the optimal step direction and size, we construct the Lagrangian for this constrained problem:
\mathcal{L}(\Delta \theta, \lambda) = g^T \Delta \theta - \lambda \left( \frac{1}{2} \Delta \theta^T H \Delta \theta - \delta \right)
We find the maximum by taking the derivative with respect to \Delta \theta and setting it to zero:
\nabla_{\Delta \theta} \mathcal{L} = g - \lambda H \Delta \theta = 0
\Delta \theta = \frac{1}{\lambda} H^{-1} g
This gives us the optimal update direction. Let the search direction be x = H^{-1} g. To find the scalar \lambda, we plug \Delta \theta back into the constraint boundary equation:
\frac{1}{2} \left( \frac{1}{\lambda} x \right)^T H \left( \frac{1}{\lambda} x \right) = \delta
\frac{1}{2 \lambda^2} x^T H x = \delta
\lambda = \sqrt{\frac{x^T H x}{2\delta}}
Finally, substituting \lambda back into the equation for \Delta \theta gives the exact parameter update:
\Delta \theta = \sqrt{\frac{2\delta}{x^T H x}} x


2.4 Bypassing the Matrix Inversion with Conjugate Gradient
The equation above requires computing x = H^{-1} g, which is equivalent to solving the linear system Hx = g.
For modern deep learning architectures, the Fisher Information Matrix H is an N \times N matrix where N is the number of network parameters. Explicitly computing, storing, and inverting this matrix is computationally intractable.
This is where the conjugate gradient (CG) method comes in. CG is an iterative algorithm for solving systems of linear equations like Hx = g without ever needing to explicitly construct the matrix H. The algorithm only requires the ability to compute matrix-vector products, specifically Hv for an arbitrary vector v.
This operation is called a Hessian-vector product (HVP). Using automatic differentiation frameworks, the HVP can be computed efficiently with two backward passes, requiring only slightly more computation than standard backpropagation:
Hv = \nabla_{\theta} \left( \left( \nabla_{\theta} \bar{D}_{KL}(\theta_{old}, \theta) \right)^T v \right)
By using the conjugate gradient method to estimate the search direction x, and then scaling it by the constraint scalar, TRPO achieves stable policy updates without the massive computational overhead of matrix inversion.


2.5 The Backtracking Algorithm
The reason TRPO needs a backtracking line search is that the math we just worked through relies heavily on local approximations. We used a first-order Taylor expansion for the objective function and a second-order approximation for the KL divergence.
To bridge the gap between the quadratic approximation and the true non-linear reality of the neural network, TRPO uses the backtracking line search. It evaluates the exact functions to guarantee the step is strictly beneficial.
Here is the step-by-step mechanics of the search:

Calculate the maximal proposed parameter update using the direction and scalar we derived earlier:
\Delta \theta = \sqrt{\frac{2\delta}{x^T H x}} x
Define a decay coefficient \alpha \in (0, 1), often set to 0.5, and initialize a decay index j = 0.
Propose a new set of policy parameters by taking a exponentially decaying fraction of the maximal step:
\theta_{new} = \theta_{old} + \alpha^j \Delta \theta
Evaluate this proposed \theta_{new} against two strict acceptance criteria using the true, unapproximated functions:
Objective improvement: L(\theta_{new}) > L(\theta_{old})
KL constraint boundary: D_{KL}(\pi_{\theta_{old}} \parallel \pi_{\theta_{new}}) \le \delta
If both conditions are satisfied, the search successfully terminates, and \theta_{new} is accepted as the new policy.
If either condition fails, it means the local approximation was too aggressive and overshot the safe region. The algorithm increments j by 1 (which shrinks the step size by another factor of \alpha) and repeats the evaluation.



2.6 Bridging the Gap with the Surrogate Objective
To understand why we can optimize a surrogate objective L(\theta) instead of the true expected return J(\theta), we need to look at their first derivatives. The foundational trick of TRPO is proving that at the exact point of the current policy parameters \theta_{old}, the gradient of the surrogate perfectly matches the gradient of the true objective.
Let’s define our terms formally:

\pi_\theta(a|s): The policy parameterized by \theta.
\theta_{old}: The current parameters of our policy before the update.
\rho_{\theta_{old}}(s): The state visitation distribution under the old policy.
A_{\theta_{old}}(s, a): The advantage function evaluated under the old policy.

First, we recall the standard Policy Gradient Theorem for our true objective J(\theta). Evaluated at the current parameters \theta_{old}, it is written as:
\nabla_\theta J(\theta)|_{\theta = \theta_{old}} = \mathbb{E}_{s \sim \rho_{\theta_{old}}, a \sim \pi_{\theta_{old}}} \left[ \nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(a|s)|_{\theta = \theta_{old}} A_{\theta_{old}}(s, a) \right]
Next, we define our surrogate objective L(\theta). This function uses importance sampling to evaluate a proposed new policy using the trajectories collected by the old policy:
L(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{s \sim \rho_{\theta_{old}}, a \sim \pi_{\theta_{old}}} \left[ \frac{\pi_\theta(a|s)}{\pi_{\theta_{old}}(a|s)} A_{\theta_{old}}(s, a) \right]
Notice the fraction in the L(\theta) equation: \frac{\pi_{\theta}(a|s)}{\pi_{\theta_{old}}(a|s)}. This is an importance sampling ratio. Because we do not know the state distribution for the proposed new policy \pi_\theta, TRPO evaluates the objective using the trajectories and state distribution already collected by the old policy \pi_{\theta_{old}}. The importance sampling ratio corrects for the fact that we are evaluating a new policy using data generated by an old one. It asks: if the new policy makes a good action more likely, how much should we increase the objective?
To find the gradient of this surrogate objective L(\theta), we take the derivative with respect to \theta. Because the expectation is taken over states and actions sampled from the old policy, the distribution over which we are taking the expectation is independent of the active variable \theta. This allows us to pass the gradient operator directly inside the expectation:
\nabla_\theta L(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{s \sim \rho_{\theta_{old}}, a \sim \pi_{\theta_{old}}} \left[ \frac{\nabla_\theta \pi_\theta(a|s)}{\pi_{\theta_{old}}(a|s)} A_{\theta_{old}}(s, a) \right]
Now, we evaluate this gradient at the exact point of our current parameters, setting \theta = \theta_{old}:
\nabla_\theta L(\theta)|_{\theta = \theta_{old}} = \mathbb{E}_{s \sim \rho_{\theta_{old}}, a \sim \pi_{\theta_{old}}} \left[ \frac{\nabla_\theta \pi_\theta(a|s)|_{\theta = \theta_{old}}}{\pi_{\theta_{old}}(a|s)} A_{\theta_{old}}(s, a) \right]
At this stage, we apply the standard log-derivative trick, which states that \nabla_x \log f(x) = \frac{\nabla_x f(x)}{f(x)}. If we apply this identity to our policy at the point \theta_{old}, we get:
\frac{\nabla_\theta \pi_\theta(a|s)|_{\theta = \theta_{old}}}{\pi_{\theta_{old}}(a|s)} = \nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(a|s)|_{\theta = \theta_{old}}
Substituting this identity back into our expectation yields our final result:
\nabla_\theta L(\theta)|_{\theta = \theta_{old}} = \mathbb{E}_{s \sim \rho_{\theta_{old}}, a \sim \pi_{\theta_{old}}} \left[ \nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(a|s)|_{\theta = \theta_{old}} A_{\theta_{old}}(s, a) \right]
This final equation is identical to the right-hand side of the Policy Gradient Theorem. Therefore, we have proven:
\nabla_\theta L(\theta)|_{\theta = \theta_{old}} = \nabla_\theta J(\theta)|_{\theta = \theta_{old}}
Because their first derivatives match, taking a small step to maximize the easy-to-calculate surrogate L(\theta) guarantees we are moving in the exact same direction as if we were maximizing the impossible-to-calculate true objective J(\theta). However, because this equality only holds strictly at \theta = \theta_{old}, we must introduce the trust region constraint to ensure we do not step too far away from this point of equivalence.


2.7 Why TRPO Uses the Fisher Information Matrix
When we use standard gradient descent to update a neural network, we are taking a step in Euclidean space. We change the parameters \theta by some small Euclidean distance \Delta \theta.
However, a neural network policy \pi_\theta(a|s) outputs a probability distribution. The relationship between the parameters and the output distribution is highly non-linear. In some regions of the parameter space, a massive change in \theta might barely affect the output probabilities. In other regions, a microscopic change in \theta might drastically shift the probabilities, completely changing the agent’s behavior and destroying the policy.
If we define our trust region simply by limiting the Euclidean distance \Delta \theta^T \Delta \theta < \epsilon, we are ignoring the actual effect on the policy. Standard gradient descent does not understand the underlying geometry of the probability distributions it is creating.
The Fisher Information Matrix solves this problem by acting as a metric tensor for probability distributions. It defines the local geometry of the probability space, often referred to as a Riemannian manifold.
Instead of measuring the Euclidean distance between parameter vectors, we want to measure the statistical distance between the resulting probability distributions. The Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence does exactly this.
If we look at the second-order Taylor expansion of the KL divergence between a policy and a slightly updated policy, a beautiful mathematical property emerges. The Hessian matrix (the matrix of second derivatives) of the KL divergence evaluated at the current parameters is exactly equal to the Fisher Information Matrix, which we will denote as F:
D_{KL}(\pi_{\theta} \parallel \pi_{\theta + \Delta \theta}) \approx \frac{1}{2} \Delta \theta^T F \Delta \theta
The FIM translates a change in parameters (\Delta \theta) into the resulting change in the probability distribution. By incorporating the FIM, TRPO transforms the standard gradient into the natural gradient. This ensures the algorithm takes steps of a consistent size in the actual behavior space, moving safely regardless of how the neural network parameters are parameterized.
TRPO explicitly substitutes the FIM into its optimization constraint to enforce the trust region. Recall the quadratic program TRPO attempts to solve. It maximizes the surrogate advantage g^T \Delta \theta subject to the KL divergence constraint. Using the relationship established above, TRPO mathematically frames the constraint using the FIM:
\frac{1}{2} \Delta \theta^T F \Delta \theta \le \delta
As derived earlier using Lagrange multipliers, the optimal step direction x for this constrained problem requires inverting this matrix:
x = F^{-1} g
This vector x is the natural gradient direction. It points toward the steepest improvement in the objective function while accounting for the curvature of the probability space defined by F.
Because the FIM is an N \times N matrix where N is the number of network parameters, explicitly constructing and inverting F is impossible for deep neural networks. TRPO uses the conjugate gradient method to approximate the solution to Fx = g. In this process, TRPO never builds the full FIM. Instead, it computes Fisher-vector products (Fv) for arbitrary vectors v.
Mathematically, the FIM is also defined as the expected outer product of the score function (the gradient of the log-probability):
F = \mathbb{E}_{s,a} \left[ \nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(a|s) \nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(a|s)^T \right]
By leveraging automatic differentiation packages, TRPO can compute the product of this massive matrix and a vector v efficiently using a sequence of vector-Jacobian products, providing the precise directional curvature needed for the natural gradient step without the impossible memory requirements.


2.8 The Monotonic Improvement Guarantee
We established that maximizing the surrogate objective L(\theta) is equivalent to maximizing the true objective J(\theta) exactly at the current parameters \theta_{old}. However, as the new policy \pi_\theta diverges from \pi_{\theta_{old}}, this approximation breaks down. If we take too large a step, an increase in L(\theta) might actually result in a catastrophic decrease in the true expected return.
To prevent this, Schulman et al. derived a theoretical lower bound that strictly bounds the difference between the true objective and the surrogate objective. They proved that the true expected return is mathematically guaranteed to be greater than or equal to the surrogate objective minus a penalty based on how much the policy distribution changes.
The theoretical lower bound is defined as:
J(\theta) \ge L(\theta) - C \max_s D_{KL}(\pi_{\theta_{old}}(\cdot|s) \parallel \pi_\theta(\cdot|s))
Let’s break down the components of this inequality:

J(\theta): The true expected return of the proposed new policy.
L(\theta): The surrogate objective evaluated using the old policy’s state distribution, \rho_{\theta_{old}}(s).
\max_s D_{KL}(\pi_{\theta_{old}}(\cdot|s) \parallel \pi_\theta(\cdot|s)): The maximum Kullback-Leibler divergence between the old and new policy across all possible states s.
C: A theoretical penalty coefficient defined as C = \frac{4\epsilon \gamma}{(1-\gamma)^2}, where \epsilon is the maximum absolute advantage and \gamma is the discount factor.

This equation is the mathematical bedrock of Trust Region Policy Optimization. It provides an absolute safety net. If we can find a new policy \theta that maximizes the right-hand side of this inequality, we are mathematically guaranteed that the true objective J(\theta) on the left-hand side will improve by at least that same amount.
By forcing the optimization process to consider the KL divergence penalty, the algorithm is mathematically prevented from taking a step that destroys the policy. It guarantees monotonic improvement.
